Attainment and Attendance across Sussex

East Sussex, West Sussex and Brighton and Hove through the national model behind How to Pull the Right Lever: one region, three different school systems. Draft for discussion.

Author
Affiliation

Adam Dennett

Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, University College London

Published

October 30, 2026

WarningDraft for discussion

This review draws together the East Sussex, West Sussex and Mid Sussex documents, and the Brighton and Hove findings of How to Pull the Right Lever. Every figure comes from published Department for Education data and the national models documented there. Nothing uses pupil-level records.

Summary

Sussex has 76 state-funded secondary schools across three local authorities and thirteen districts. Taken together in 2024-25:

  • Results: 45.4 in Attainment 8, against 46.9 for England.
  • Disadvantaged pupils: 33.4 against 37.8.
  • Disadvantage: 21.5% of pupils are disadvantaged, against 28.3% nationally.

Sussex is less disadvantaged than England, does a little less well overall, and does markedly less well by its disadvantaged pupils. The findings:

  • The disadvantaged shortfall is the region’s shared problem. Every one of the three authorities is below England for its disadvantaged pupils. The largest single cause is being in the South East (1.3 points). Of England’s nine regions, the South East has the most negative regional effect for disadvantaged pupils. Absence and prior attainment add to it.
  • Beneath that, three different systems.
    • Brighton and Hove has effective schools held back by absence far beyond what its intake predicts.
    • East Sussex has schools that do about what is expected, pupils with lower prior attainment, and the absence its intake predicts.
    • West Sussex has an advantaged intake, ordinary attendance, and schools below expectation, most of all for disadvantaged pupils.
  • Illness drives Sussex’s excess absence everywhere. All three authorities record more illness absence than England, Brighton and Hove most of all. Reduced timetables run above the national rate in East and West Sussex.
  • The practice gaps are large and specific. East Sussex suspends at twice Brighton and Hove’s rate, and West Sussex uses reduced timetables at about twice the national rate.
  • Place matters within the region, but mostly as schools. Average value added runs from +2.4 points in Worthing to -3.6 in Hastings. But only Crawley has a district effect that survives once each school’s own record is counted.
  • Trusts matter about as much as local authorities, more for disadvantaged pupils and attendance. United Learning runs schools in both counties and stands out for results. Ark (Hastings) stands out for disadvantaged pupils and attendance. Kemnal (West Sussex) and Aldridge (Brighton and Hove) run significantly more absence than their intakes predict.
  • In none of the three does the mix of pupils between schools explain results. Attendance, prior attainment, and what happens inside particular schools do.

1 About this review

The three authority-level documents each apply the published national models to one authority. This review sets them side by side and adds the view of Sussex as one system. Two things should be borne in mind:

  • Sussex is not an administrative unit for schools. Its three authorities have their own admissions, school improvement and attendance services. “Sussex” here is a lens, not a governing body.
  • Brighton and Hove is the subject of the Lever report itself. Its figures here come from the same models and data.

The methods are described in full in the East Sussex document.

2 Sussex’s schools

Sussex’s 76 state-funded secondary schools, coloured by overall absence in 2024/25, within its thirteen districts. Choose another measure from the menu above the map; circle size is the school’s roll. Hover for figures and who runs each school.

The three authorities run their schools very differently:

  • Brighton and Hove maintains seven of its ten.
  • West Sussex maintains nearly half.
  • East Sussex has most of its schools in 11 different multi-academy trusts.

Two trusts, United Learning and the University of Brighton Academies Trust, ran schools in both counties in 2024/25.

Read across the two tables, the three authorities are three distinct cases:

  • Brighton and Hove is the strongest on the model: its schools are 5th in England once intake is accounted for. It is also the most dependent on absence: it falls from 15th to 69th for disadvantaged pupils without the absence control, because its absence is the 3rd furthest above its intake in England.
  • East Sussex is in the middle on every measure. Its schools do what is expected, and its absence is what its intake predicts.
  • West Sussex is the reverse of Brighton and Hove: absence is ordinary, and its schools sit significantly below expectation for disadvantaged pupils (131st of 151).

4 What explains attainment across Sussex

The decomposition for Sussex as a whole, in Attainment 8 points.
Factor All pupils Disadvantaged Non-disadvantaged
Absence -0.63 -0.69 -0.50
Prior attainment (KS2) -0.57 -0.33 -0.46
Place (region and local authority) -0.41 -1.78 -0.38
English as an additional language -0.13 -0.36 -0.19
Ofsted rating +0.03 +0.03 +0.03
Unexplained (school residual) +0.08 +0.01 +0.05
Teacher workforce +0.11 -0.02 +0.10
Other model terms +0.13 -0.32 +0.11
Disadvantage (% FSM) +0.49 -0.18 +0.27

Sussex as a whole is 0.9 points below England for all pupils. Its low disadvantage lifts it (+0.49), and three things pull it down:

  • absence (-0.63);
  • prior attainment (-0.57);
  • being in the South East (-0.46).

The three authorities’ own effects roughly cancel. Brighton and Hove’s positive effect offsets West Sussex’s negative one.

For disadvantaged pupils Sussex is 3.5 points below England. The largest single piece is the region (-1.32), followed by absence (-0.69) and the authorities’ own effects (-0.46, mostly West Sussex’s).

The regional effect is not something any one authority can change, but it is real and it is shared. Of England’s nine regions, the South East has the most negative effect for disadvantaged pupils: they do less well there than equally disadvantaged pupils elsewhere with the same prior attainment and attendance. That is a regional question as much as a local one.

5 Place: authorities and districts

Value added differs widely between districts, and the two ends tell different stories:

  • Hastings and Crawley have the lowest value added, and very different intakes. Hastings is Sussex’s most disadvantaged district; Crawley’s disadvantage is near the county average.
  • In Hastings, the low figure is two schools. With each school’s own record in the model, no district effect remains.
  • In Crawley, every school is below expectation, and for non-disadvantaged pupils the district effect survives the school term. It is the closest thing in Sussex to a genuine place effect.
  • Worthing and Lewes are at the top. Both have some of the region’s strongest individual schools, and neither has a district effect once those schools are counted.

The lesson is consistent across the region. A district is a useful way to see where difficulties gather, but in all but one case the difficulty belongs to particular schools, not to the place.

6 Trusts across Sussex

In 2024/25, 23 multi-academy trusts ran Sussex secondary schools, most of them one or two schools each. The trust analysis in the East Sussex document estimates every trust’s effect across all its secondary schools in England. It allows for each school’s own record and for whether it was sponsored. Nationally, a trust moves results by about 2.2%, about as much as a local authority, and absence by about 6.7%.

Four of the trusts running Sussex schools stand out nationally:

  • Above average:
    • for all pupils: United Learning Trust;
    • for disadvantaged pupils: Ark Schools, United Learning Trust.
  • Absence below what their intakes predict: Ark Schools.
  • Absence above what their intakes predict: Aldridge Education, The Kemnal Academies Trust.

Most of the rest are small trusts that cannot be separated from their one or two schools.

Nothing here suggests that academies as a group do better or worse than maintained schools in Sussex. Nationally, the differences by route are a percent or two once intake is allowed for. The region’s strongest schools on value added are a mix of maintained schools (St Oscar Romero, St Richard’s, Downlands) and academies (King’s Academy Ringmer, Durrington, Steyning).

7 Absence across Sussex

In autumn and spring 2025/26:

  • Brighton and Hove: 9.8%, 6th highest in England.
  • East Sussex: 8.9%, 31st, falling fast.
  • West Sussex: 8.1%, 70th, close to England’s 8.0%.

Only Brighton and Hove’s is much above what its intake predicts.

The table shows three things:

  • Illness is the shared problem. It is above England’s rate everywhere, and in Brighton and Hove by a margin (5.42% against 3.67%). The published data cannot say what lies behind it. All three authorities’ own records could, and comparing them is the obvious first step.
  • Reduced timetables are West Sussex’s outlier, at 1.9 times England’s rate.
  • Suspension is East Sussex’s outlier, at 28.0 per 100 pupils against 13.0 in Brighton and Hove. Neighbouring authorities with similar pupils make very different decisions about exclusion, which suggests these are choices that can be changed.

8 School by school

Across Sussex’s schools the two signals move together (correlation -0.58). The schools furthest out are named.

  • Strongest: St Oscar Romero (Worthing), St Richard’s (Bexhill) and King’s Academy Ringmer.
  • Weakest: Thomas Bennett (Crawley), the two Hastings academies, and The Littlehampton Academy.

Both Hastings academies have since moved to a new trust.

9 Implications for Sussex

  1. Disadvantaged pupils are the regional priority. All three authorities are below England for them. A part of the shortfall is regional and shared, and so is the case for working on it together.
  2. Each authority has a different first lever.
    • Brighton and Hove: attendance, and finding out why its absence is so far above its intake.
    • East Sussex: attendance, prior attainment, and its high suspension rate.
    • West Sussex: what happens inside its schools for disadvantaged pupils, starting with Crawley.
    A single Sussex-wide prescription would fit none of them.
  3. Illness absence is common to all three, and their combined records could show what lies behind it in a way no one authority’s could.
  4. Practice varies more than intake does. Suspension in East Sussex and reduced timetables in West Sussex are choices made within the system, and neighbouring authorities make them differently.
  5. Schools, not structures, carry most of the variation. Districts and trusts matter at the margin. The strongest effects in every analysis here belong to individual schools. Learning from the region’s best schools is the most direct lever available, and those schools include maintained schools and academies alike.

Notes on method

Methods and sources are those of the East Sussex document. “Sussex” figures are means over all 76 schools (for school-level measures) or sums over their sessions and pupils (for absence and suspensions). This review is built by R/17_area_analysis.R, R/18_district_effects.R, R/19_trust_effects.R, R/19b_sussex_boundaries.R and sussex_review.qmd.
